name: Cinnamon / apple cider vinegar shots

card.summary: Diluted apple cider vinegar (sometimes with cinnamon) taken for fat loss and skin; no high-quality trials back the appearance claims.
card.note: Undiluted or excessive vinegar is reported to damage tooth enamel and irritate the throat.

quick.overview:
ACV shots are small servings of diluted apple cider vinegar, sometimes mixed with cinnamon, drunk in the hope of losing fat, reducing bloating or clearing skin.

Wikipedia reports no high-quality clinical evidence that regular use affects body weight or blood sugar and lipids, and that health organizations do not recommend it as a therapy.
quick.mechanism: Proponents attribute effects to acetic acid, which they say curbs appetite and moderates blood sugar. Published high-quality evidence for these effects in appearance terms was not found.
quick.risks: Diluted moderate use is generally described as low-risk. Reported harms include tooth-enamel erosion, throat and esophageal irritation, digestive upset, and burns when applied to skin or eyes. Possible interactions with insulin and diuretics are noted.

lead: Cinnamon and apple cider vinegar (ACV) shots are a home-made drink in which diluted apple cider vinegar, sometimes with cinnamon, is swallowed in the hope of a leaner midsection, less bloating and clearer skin. Practitioners use it as a daily morning or pre-meal routine, on the reasoning that vinegar and cinnamon blunt blood-sugar spikes and appetite, which in turn supports fat loss and a leaner look.[1][2]

Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting pressed apple juice first to alcohol and then to acetic acid; it is about 94% water and 5% acetic acid, with 22 kcal per 100 g.[1] Cinnamon is the bark of Cinnamomum trees; most commercial cinnamon is cassia, while Ceylon (true) cinnamon comes mainly from Sri Lanka.[2] Vinegar has been used in folk medicine since antiquity, and wellness routines built around it are a modern continuation of that tradition.[9]

Research on the two ingredients is mostly about metabolic markers rather than appearance. A 12-week Japanese trial in obese adults reported lower body weight, visceral fat and waist circumference with daily vinegar than with placebo drink, while Wikipedia reports no high-quality clinical evidence that regular vinegar use helps with body weight or blood glucose and lipids, and that major public-health organizations do not recommend it as a therapy.[1][10] For cinnamon, a 2012 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for diabetes, while a 2023 meta-analysis of meta-analyses reported modest reductions in fasting glucose and HbA1c.[2]

paras: The routine usually involves a small amount of apple cider vinegar diluted in water, sometimes with cinnamon or lemon, taken in the morning or before a meal. Proponents expect less bloating, fewer cravings and steadier energy, which they connect to a flatter-looking stomach and better skin.

Variants include vinegar-only drinks, vinegar with ground cinnamon or cinnamon sticks steeped in the water, and vinegar added to tea or sparkling water. Vinegar is also sold as capsules, tablets and gummies, and Wikipedia reports that esophageal injury has been documented with vinegar tablets and that commercial products vary in acidity.[1][9]

A shot generally means a small amount of vinegar diluted in water, with cinnamon added in some recipes. Apple cider vinegar is made by yeast fermentation of apple juice to cider, followed by acetic acid bacteria (Acetobacter) converting the alcohol to acetic acid; unfiltered versions may keep a cellulose "mother" biofilm.[1] It has long been used in dressings, marinades and preserves, and recipes for it appear in 19th-century cookbooks.[1]

Folk medicine has used vinegar since antiquity; Wikipedia cites Babylonian culinary and medicinal use around 3000 BCE and describes medicinal uses in the Chinese agricultural manual Qimin Yaoshu.[9] Fruit vinegars became popular in the North Atlantic in the early 1800s, and an 1810 cookbook by Esther Copley included apple cider vinegar recipes.[1] Cinnamon has its own long history as a spice and medicinal bark, and its trade shaped early modern commerce.[2]
The pairing of the two in a morning shot is a contemporary wellness practice; the sources cited here do not identify a single originator.

Claimed benefits include weight loss, reduced bloating, blood sugar and cholesterol control, and improved skin.[1] Cinnamon is added for flavour and for claimed effects on blood sugar and appetite, a link examined mainly in people with diabetes.[2][3] Wikipedia says the evidence for vinegar in skin infections is also poor.[1]

Cassia cinnamon contains more coumarin than Ceylon cinnamon, a compound that can affect the liver at high intakes. EFSA set a tolerable daily intake of 0.1 mg per kg body weight in 2008, equal to roughly 0.4 g of high-coumarin cassia per day for a 50 kg adult.[2] Reported side effects of cinnamon are mainly gastrointestinal upset and allergic reactions.[2]

A randomised, double-blind 12-week trial in obese Japanese adults (Kondo and colleagues, 2009) assigned participants to a drink containing a lower or higher amount of vinegar or to a placebo drink with no vinegar; both vinegar groups had lower body weight, BMI, visceral fat area, waist circumference and serum triglycerides than placebo, and the authors concluded daily vinegar might help prevent metabolic syndrome by reducing obesity.[10]

A 2020 systematic review in the European Journal of Nutrition by Launholt and colleagues searched four databases, identified 487 papers and included 13 human and 12 animal studies; the authors concluded apple vinegar may have beneficial effects and that side-effect risk appears small at recommended amounts, but called the evidence insufficient and asked for larger, long-term, low-bias trials.[11] Wikipedia uses that review to say side effects appear unlikely at moderate diluted intake while stating that no high-quality clinical evidence shows benefit for body weight.[1]

A 2024 trial in BMJ Nutrition, Prevention and Health in 120 Lebanese adolescents and young adults with overweight or obesity assigned participants to one of three daily ACV amounts or placebo for 12 weeks and reported reductions in weight, BMI, waist and hip circumference, body fat ratio, glucose and lipids; that paper was later retracted, with a retraction notice published in September 2025.[12] A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis in Nutrients examined ACV and body composition in adults with overweight or type 2 diabetes, and a 2026 randomised trial in Scientific Reports tested ACV added to metformin in women with polycystic ovary syndrome.[13]
A preliminary line of research reported that 2 to 4 tablespoons of vinegar may modestly reduce post-meal glucose and insulin in people with diabetes, per Wikipedia's summary.[9]

For cinnamon, a 2024 meta-analysis of 24 randomized trials in type 2 diabetes pooled reductions in fasting blood sugar, insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) and HbA1c versus controls, with no significant change in insulin, while the authors described the overall glycemic effect as inconclusive.[3] A 2003 trial of 60 people with type 2 diabetes randomised them to 1, 3 or 6 g of cinnamon daily or placebo capsules and measured glucose and lipids.[4] A 2024 four-week crossover trial examined cinnamon and continuously monitored glucose response in adults with prediabetes.[5] Other randomised trials have tested cinnamon in type 2 diabetes,[6] Ceylon cinnamon specifically,[7] and an aqueous cinnamon extract on after-meal glucose.[8]
All of these trials measured blood sugar or lipids rather than waist size or skin. No published trials were found of the combined vinegar-and-cinnamon shot for appearance or skin.

Wikipedia lists tooth-enamel damage from large quantities, esophageal damage from incompletely swallowed tablets, more burping and flatulence, increased tooth sensitivity, possible interactions with insulin or diuretics, and possible allergy in people with apple allergy; topical use on skin may cause burns.[1] Moderate, diluted consumption was considered low-risk in the 2020 review.[1][11]

Wikipedia also notes irritation and possible corneal injury if vinegar contacts the eyes, variable acid concentration between brands, mould and yeast contamination found in some products, and that vinegar may be unsafe for pregnant or breastfeeding women and children.[1] Vinegar solutions above 10 percent are described as corrosive to skin, and vinegar sold for medicinal purposes is not standardised.[9]

A 2022 in vitro study of acidic beverages and dietary preservatives on extracted human teeth reported that vinegar and apple cider caused the greatest demineralisation overall, affecting both enamel and dentin.[14]

lore.intro: Claims about ACV and cinnamon shots circulate widely in wellness circles and appearance communities as a simple daily habit for a leaner waist, less bloating and better skin; the benefits listed below are those described in reference summaries of the claimed uses.[1][2]

claims.claim: A daily ACV shot helps burn fat and slim the waist.
claims.believers: Proponents say vinegar curbs appetite and moderates blood sugar, so they eat less and carry less belly fat.[1] Some point to the Japanese 2009 trial of daily vinegar in obese adults.[10]
claims.experts: That trial reported lower weight and visceral fat, but the Launholt 2020 review judged the overall evidence insufficient and Wikipedia reports no high-quality clinical evidence for body-weight benefit; a 2024 trial reporting benefit was retracted.[1][10][11][12]

claims.claim: Vinegar and cinnamon steady blood sugar, which reduces cravings and bloating.
claims.believers: Proponents say the pair moderates post-meal glucose so energy and appetite stay steadier.[1][2]
claims.experts: Cinnamon trials in diabetes show modest pooled reductions in glucose markers but the authors call the overall effect inconclusive; vinegar may modestly reduce post-meal glucose in people with diabetes.[3][9]

claims.believers: Proponents list clearer skin among the benefits of the daily shot.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says the evidence for vinegar even in skin infections is poor, and no published trial of oral ACV shots for skin appearance was found.[1]

claims.claim: Diluted shots are harmless, but undiluted vinegar or tablets can cause harm.
claims.believers: Users commonly stress dilution and rinsing the mouth as part of the routine.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists enamel damage, throat and esophageal injury from tablets, and possible interactions with insulin or diuretics; an in vitro study found vinegar and apple cider caused the most demineralisation of teeth among acidic items tested.[1][14]

claims.claim: Ceylon cinnamon is a safer choice than cassia for daily use.
claims.believers: Practitioners prefer Ceylon cinnamon because they have heard cassia can strain the liver.[2]
claims.experts: Cassia contains more coumarin, and EFSA's 2008 tolerable intake of 0.1 mg per kg body weight equals roughly 0.4 g of high-coumarin cassia daily for a 50 kg adult.[2]
